n: God tests Abraham. “Tempt” here means to test or prove, not to lure into sin. Abraham answers with ready willingness: “Here I am.”

f.g: Test or prove (Hebrew nissah). God does not entice to evil (James 1:13).
Hebrew hinneni — a reply of readiness and availability.

n: God’s command builds in painful steps: your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love. Abraham is asked to offer the very son through whom God’s promises were to come. Latter-day Saints see this as a likeness of the Father offering His Only Begotten Son.

f.w: thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest

f.g: Later identified as the mountain where Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 3:1).

n: Abraham rises early and obeys without recorded argument. He prepares the wood himself and sets out.

f.g: A sign of prompt obedience (compare 21:14).
Split; chopped.

n: On the third day Abraham sees the place in the distance. For three days Isaac was, in Abraham’s heart, as good as dead—many see a parallel to Christ’s three days in the tomb.
Abraham tells the servants that he and the boy will worship and come back. Hebrews says Abraham believed God could raise Isaac from the dead.

f.g: Hebrew “we will return”—plural.

n: Isaac carries the wood up the mountain, as Jesus would later carry His cross. Father and son walk on together.

f.w: laid it upon Isaac his son
they went both of them together
f.g: Repeated in verse 8—father and son united in purpose.

n: Isaac asks the poignant question: “Where is the lamb?” The question echoes through scripture until John the Baptist points to Jesus.

f.w: where is the lamb for a burnt offering?

n: Abraham answers in faith: God will provide the lamb. His words point beyond the moment to the Lamb God would provide for the world.

f.w: God will provide himself a lamb
f.g: Can also be read “God will provide Himself as the lamb.”

n: Abraham builds the altar, arranges the wood, binds Isaac, and lays him on it. Isaac, likely a young man strong enough to carry wood, seems to submit willingly—like Christ.

f.g: Jewish tradition calls this story the Aqedah, “the binding.”

n: Abraham raises the knife. The text slows down to let us feel the terrible moment.

f.g: Abraham fully intends to obey.

n: The angel of the Lord calls urgently, “Abraham, Abraham!” Abraham again answers, “Here am I.”

f.g: A doubled name signals urgency and intimacy (compare Exodus 3:4; 1 Samuel 3:10).

n: The angel stops him: Abraham has proven his reverence for God by not holding back his son. God never intended Isaac’s death; human sacrifice is condemned elsewhere in scripture.

f.w: now I know that thou fearest God
Lay not thine hand upon the lad

n: Abraham sees a ram caught in a thicket and offers it in Isaac’s place. A substitute dies so the son can live—an image of Christ’s atoning sacrifice for us.

f.w: in the stead of his son
f.g: In place of his son—a picture of substitution.
Dense bushes.

n: Abraham names the place “the LORD will provide” (or “see”). The saying “in the mount of the LORD it shall be seen” anticipates the temple on this mountain and the Savior’s sacrifice nearby.

f.g: “The LORD will see” or “the LORD will provide.”

f.w: In the mount of the LORD

n: The angel calls a second time with a renewed promise.

f.g: The test is followed by blessing.

n: God swears by Himself—there is no one greater to swear by. Because Abraham did not withhold his son, the covenant is solemnly confirmed.
Abraham’s descendants will be as countless as stars and sand, and they will overcome their enemies. Latter-day revelation applies these promises to Abraham’s eternal increase.

f.w: as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore
possess the gate of his enemies
f.g: Control their enemies’ cities—a sign of victory.

n: Through Abraham’s seed all nations will be blessed. Peter and Paul taught that this promise is fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

f.w: in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed

n: Abraham returns with Isaac to the servants, and they go home to Beersheba.
News arrives about Abraham’s brother Nahor’s family back in Mesopotamia. This short genealogy prepares for Isaac’s marriage in chapter 24.
Nahor’s sons include Huz and Buz—names linked with desert regions—and Kemuel.

f.g: The same name as Uz, Job’s homeland (Job 1:1).

n: The list continues, ending with Bethuel, the key figure for the next story.

f.g: Possibly ancestor of the Chaldeans (Kasdim).

n: Bethuel fathers Rebekah, Isaac’s future wife. Even as Abraham’s test ends, God is preparing the next step.
Nahor also has sons by a secondary wife. In total he has twelve sons—like Ishmael and Jacob after him.

f.g: A secondary wife with lower status, whose children could still be legitimate heirs.
Also the name of an Aramean region (2 Samuel 10:6).
